tagline: NASA pad at Cape Canaveral (1961-68) — first Saturn I; Apollo 1 fire site 1967-01-27; Apollo 7 first crewed launch 1968-10-11
dispatch: Launch Complex 34 is where the Saturn era began — and where it almost ended. The first Saturn rocket lifted off from this single-towered pad in 1961, proving von Braun's outsized boosters could fly at all. It is also the place where, on 27 January 1967, the Apollo 1 fire killed Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee during a ground test — the program's darkest day, on the pad, before anything had left the ground. And it is where Apollo came back twenty-one months later: Apollo 7, the first crewed flight, launched from LC-34 and proved the redesigned spacecraft was sound. One small pad held the whole arc — the beginning, the catastrophe, and the recovery. A memorial stands there now.
description: Cape Canaveral Launch Complex 34 served NASA from 1961-10-27 (first Saturn I, SA-1) through 1968-10-11 (Apollo 7, the first crewed Apollo flight). LC-34's single steel umbilical tower hosted four uncrewed Saturn I flights (SA-1 through SA-4, 1961-1963), was then reconstructed for Saturn IB, and flew two uncrewed Saturn IB flights (AS-201 in 1966, AS-202 in 1966) before the Apollo 1 test. On 1967-01-27 during a Plugs-Out test of Apollo 1 — the planned first crewed Block I CSM flight — a flash fire in the pure-O₂ cabin killed Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee in seconds. The pad was rebuilt for Apollo 7 (1968-10-11) which launched the first crewed Apollo flight, then deactivated 1968-11. The pad's concrete deluge ring + main flame trench still stand; a memorial plaque on site reads "They gave their lives in service to their country in the ongoing exploration of humankind's final frontier."
